newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines asked to improve corn yields.
newsitem.headline: Philippines asked to improve corn yields.

text.p: Philippine meat processors and livestock raisers urged the government on Thursday to invest in improving the country's corn yields so their products could be made cheaper to face competition from cheap imports.

"Due to local corn insufficiency and high duties of imported corn and corn substitutes, the local animal industries are disadvantaged against imported meat products," the Philippine Association of Feedmillers Inc (PAFMI) said in a position paper submitted to President Fidel Ramos.

PAMPI and other groups from the local meat processors, corn farmers and livestock producers submitted proposals on how the government can help their industries meet competition from cheaper imported meat products in a forum on Thursday.
Local feed millers and livestock groups said local corn production continued to lag behind demand due to declining corn lands, insufficient facilities, and lack of transport services.
Corn substitutes are also slapped with very high duties, the lowest of which is currently pegged at 35 percent of the total cost of the imported commodity, PAMPI said.

The country's corn lands dropped to 2.69 million hectares in 1995 from the 1990 level of 3.82 million as marginal corn farmers shifted to more profitable crops, the Federation of Free Farmers, the country's largest farmers' cooperative, said.
The farmers' group said the country's average yellow corn yield remain substantially below "world class levels," of five million tonnes per hectare.
"The low yields and high cost of production of corn farmers place them at peril against cheaper corn imports," the farmers' group said in their position paper.

"An in-depth study must be made to determine the actual and projected comparative advantage of the country in the production of corn feeds. The findings may indicate that world class corn production can be pursued only in selected parts of the country," the Federation of Free Farmers said.
Livestock raisers said the high cost of corn for feeds have made locally produced meat products less competitive.
"Corn accounts for 60 percent of broiler cost. If corn prices remain, so will poultry products," the Philippine Association of Broiler Integrators Inc said.
